newsitem.title: UK: London gold slightly firmer in range-bound market.
newsitem.headline: London gold slightly firmer in range-bound market.

text.p: Precious metal prices were mixed on Thursday afternoon but remained within narrow prices ranges following a mixed opening in New York.
Dealers said the markets were mostly quiet and trading with their ranges for lack of investor attention.
"There's just not much going on this afternoon. The dollar is a little easier but it hasn't helped gold," one dealer said.
Gold was fixed at $319.40 per ounce up from $318.75 this morning. Around the fixing the August contract on New York's Comex gold futures market was up $1.70 at $320.40.
Some dealers said the pattern recently had been for the Europeans to buy the markets only for New York to sell it down later in the day.
On Wednesday that happened most conspicuously with silver which had been tipped for a try at $4.40 per ounce in Europe.
In the event failed it to get beyond $4.30 and finally was sold off by the investment funds to about 10 cents under the London close.
Now dealers were forecasting another assault by the funds aiming at getting silver down to a target of $4.00.
At its midday fixing it was set at $4.2235, its lowest fixing since November 3, 1993 of $4.2125.
Dealers said the precious metals were being outshone by the world's stockmarkets which were at or near record levels.

Gold prices have been under pressure all year and the pressure increased at the beginning of this month when the Australian central bank announced it had sold 167 tonnes of gold from its reserves over the previous six months.
The news dropped the gold price to 12-year lows and brought several mines to the point were they cannot cover costs.
The investment funds which set the price rolling down after the Australian news, have gone short to extend Comex open interest to levels not seen since the February 1996 bull rally.
Borrowing to cover these short positions is becoming more expensive as the squeeze on material has sent one month implied lease rates to over 2.50 percent.

That is a fraction of the cost to borrow platinum and palladium which were quoted at 30 percent and 75 percent respectively for a month today reflecting the continuous tightness caused by leading exporter Russia only now beginning its 1997 export schedule.
Spot platinum was indicated at $401.00/$404.00 down $4.00 and palladium was at $174.50/$177.50 down $2.25.
